title: Greg Sherwood MW: 2021 – the Cape’s next great Cab vintage
summary:
If you have been following numerous wine commentators and wine social media accounts of late, you would have found it pretty difficult to miss all the debates comparing the 2015 to the 2017 vintage in the Cape. Without a question of a doubt, both are vintages that are developing into two of South Africa’s most […]

The post Greg Sherwood MW: 2021 – the Cape’s next great Cab vintage appeared first on winemag.
content:
If you have been following numerous wine commentators and wine social media accounts of late, you would have found it pretty difficult to miss all the debates comparing the 2015 to the 2017 vintage in the Cape.

Without a question of a doubt, both are vintages that are developing into two of South Africa’s most revered and collectable. As 2017 hits the ten-year mark in a few months’ time, this debate is sure to intensify further – the ten-year landmark normally regarded as a key quality marker for assessing the Cape’s top reds.

Indeed, I’d be lying if I said I wasn’t also quite drawn to a recent blind tasting held by famous South African sommelier, Higgo Jacobs, where he compared the 2015 and the 2017 releases of Meerlust Rubicon, Stark Condé Three Pines, Kanonkop Paul Sauer and Glenelly Lady May Cape Bordeaux blends. At nine years and eleven years old respectively, it seems a good time to make some new ageing assessments as many consumers and collectors alike will be thinking about starting to pull corks, if they haven’t started doing so already.

2015 vs 2017: The debate continues

Looking at the results, they certainly seemed to be inconclusive. The Meerlust Rubicon 2015 – a legendary wine – was considered “cracking” and preferred to the 2017. The Stark Condé Three Pines 2015 was also preferred over the 2017. For the Kanonkop Paul Sauer, the adjudication was a little closer, the 2017 Paul Sauer just pipping the famous Tim Atkin MW 100-point 2015, though both were noted as being the “wines of the night.” Finally, the exceptional 2017 Lady May was also preferred over the 2015, but it was noted that the wines both shared many similarities.

The conclusions drawn from this little tasting was that the differences between the two vintages, when tasted blind, was not as easy to distinguish as would be expected. More importantly, out of the eight wines, all were considered still in an upward trajectory of development and can, or should, be cellared for longer. Both vintages are living up to expectations as collectable fine wines for the long haul.

2021 – the next one to watch

But with very few of these wines still on the market, I thought it would be far more helpful and insightful for Winemag.co.za readers to highlight another recent tasting I went to in London – The Cabernet Collective’s Stellenbosch Vintage 2021 Tasting – held at the ‘new’ mecca of South African fine dining and fine wine, Kudu Restaurant at 7 Moxon Street, Marylebone. (Do pop in for lunch or dinner if you are visiting London, and ask for Brian Tapera, the very capable Zimbabwean sommelier!)

For those that don’t know, the Stellenbosch Cabernet Collective is a group of Stellenbosch producers brought together with the aim of “curating the expression of Stellenbosch through Cabernet Sauvignon”. They are joined together in sharing passion, discovery and knowledge. “It is to Stellenbosch that we look for the classic and elegant Cabernet Sauvignons that sit comfortably on the global stage, shoulder to shoulder with the world’s most revered wines,” organizer Billie Lambrechts will tell you.

As a reminder, the 2020 post-harvest period was characterised by very hot and dry conditions, which led to early leaf fall, especially in early ripening cultivars. The winter rainfall started late, but regular cold fronts contributed almost 100mm more precipitation than in the previous season. The budding period was particularly cool and wet, and low soil temperatures delayed bud break by up to 14 days, with bud break for later cultivars such as Cabernet Sauvignon developing evenly.

Despite sustained cool conditions, the flowering and fruit set periods were moderate and ideal. Véraison followed the seasonal trend and was generally up to 14 days later than the previous season. Ripening was consistently about 10-14 days later than the previous year, and the ripening period was very moderate. This resulted in good hang times, minimal harvesting pressure and allowed for optimal picking.

Although yields were lower, the grape compositions and preliminary wine quality of the 2021 vintage showed immediate promise. Despite the cooler conditions, the red cultivars generally achieved ideal sugar and alcohol levels, with lower pHs and higher acidities than in other recent seasons. The wines, overall, have intensity and freshness coupled with very fine, linear tannin structures – all the building blocks for yet another excellent, ageworthy Cape vintage.

Top five

1 – Tied

Le Riche Reserve 2021, 14.5% – Dense and intense, perfumed with cassis and violets, salty crème de cassis, black cherries and dusty stony minerality. Full and impressive in the mouth, satin texture with a bold concentration, plush mineral tannins and a focused, powerful finish. Wow! True class. 97/100 GSMW

1 – Tied

Thelema Mountain Vineyards Cabernet Sauvignon 2021, 14% Abv. – Beautifully seductive perfume of violets, black currants and black cherry kirsch liquor. Super polished marble tannins, tight knit, fine grained and simply delicious. Well integrated acids lend extra frame and linearity before a tart, vibrant, tangy black berry laden finish. Simply benchmark! 97/100 GSMW

2

Oldenburg Rondekop Per Se 2021, 14.64% Abv. – This is a classy, slightly broody expression of top-class Cab, showing violet and white flower perfume, notable minerality and layers of earthy black berry fruits, saline cassis, cherry pipe tobacco, and delicate cedar notes. The palate is taut and polished, effortlessly weightless and bright with a tight grained classy finessed finish. Very smart indeed. 96+/100 GSMW

3 – Tied

Meerlust 2021, 13.7% Abv. – Tight and broody, this has closed up into a more mineral expression with graphite and cedar, crushed stones, black berries and black orchard fruits. Sleek and subtle, this suggests a lot but is holding back the full fireworks. Texture of silk, fabulous tension and beautifully fine-grained tannins with a wet stone minerality on the finish. Very serious and seriously classy. 96/100 GSMW

3 – Tied

Bellevue Reserve 2021, 14% Abv. – Rich exotic black fruits layer the palate supported by an attractive perfume of violets, cherry blossom and sweet blueberries. The palate is so polished and fine with chalky tannins, a super fine-grained texture and a harmonious focused finish. Real class. 96/100 GSMW

4

Delaire Graff Reserve 2021, 14.8% Abv. – A masterclass from Morne Vrey, this is complex and multi-dimensional with aromatics of cigar box, oyster shell, graphite and kelp over salty black currant notes. Super polished and sleek, the palate is elegantly fleshy and opulent with a pinpoint focus, chalky granitic tannins, and a cool, taut mineral finish. A very grown-up expression. 95+/100 GSMW

5 – Tied

Cavalli 2021, Helderberg, 14.55% Abv. – Exoticly perfumed nose with violets and white blossoms, red and black currants and subtle hints of sour plum. Cool, creamy and silky with sweet tannins, a delightful tight grained tension, and a pitch perfect balance on the spicy finish. Delightful. 95/100 GSMW

5 – Tied

Journey’s End V4 2021, Helderberg, 14% Abv. – Classical aromatics with violets and cedar spice, potpourri and black currant fruit notes. Silky mouthfeel, real precision and focus, satin tannins but tight knit with an intense persistent concentration on the mineral-laden finish. Top Drawer kit. 95/100 GSMW

Best of the rest:

Alto 2021, Helderberg, 14.5% Abv. – 94+/100 GSMW

Ernie Els Wines Major Series 2021, Helderberg, 13.95% Abv. – 94+/100 GSMW

Rust en Vrede 2021, Helderberg, 14% Abv. – 94+/100 GSMW

Klein Graniet 2021, 14% Abv. – 94+/100 GSMW

Le Riche 2021, Faure, 14.39% Abv. – 94/100 GSMW

Avontuur The West Peak 2021, 14.34% Abv. – 93+/100 GSMW

Waterford 2021, 13.5% Abv. – 93+/100 GSMW

  • Greg Sherwood was born in Pretoria, South Africa, and as the son of a career diplomat, spent his first 21 years traveling the globe with his parents. With a Business Management and Marketing degree from Webster University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA, Sherwood began his working career as a commodity trader. In 2000, he decided to make more of a long-held interest in wine taking a position at Handford Wines in South Kensington, London, working his way up to the position of Senior Wine Buyer over 22 years. Sherwood currently consults to a number of top fine wine merchants in London while always keeping one eye firmly on the South African wine industry. He qualified as the 303rd Master of Wine in 2007.

The post NFB Old Vine Report 2026: Call for entries appeared first on winemag.
content:
Entries for the third annual Old Vine Report are now open, with NFB Private Wealth Management, established in 1985, joining as sponsor.

Wines must be made from Certified Heritage Vineyards (vines that are 35 years and older vines registered with SAWIS and approved by the Old Vine Project).

The report will be based on the outcome of a blind tasting of wines entered within a specific category and includes key findings, tasting notes for the Top 10 wines, buyer’s guide and scores on the 100-point quality scale for all wines entered.

Wines will be tasted by a three-person panel consisting of Christian Eedes as chairman, James Pietersen, CEO of of Wine Cellar, Cape Town merchants and cellarers of fine wine, and Francois Rautenbach, a hospitality and wine specialist, scoring done according to the 100-point system.

title: Tim James: America has discovered Chenin. Again.
summary:
Something like “The Great Chenin Blanc Renaissance” has been a common article title here for a few decades now. But the one published recently on Wine-searcher was primarily about America. There, according to one quoted Napa restaurateur and wine shop owner, “chenin for a long time was pretty bad. Now it‘s spectacular.” One of the producers […]

The post Tim James: America has discovered Chenin. Again. appeared first on winemag.
content:
Something like “The Great Chenin Blanc Renaissance” has been a common article title here for a few decades now. But the one published recently on Wine-searcher was primarily about America. There, according to one quoted Napa restaurateur and wine shop owner, “chenin for a long time was pretty bad. Now it‘s spectacular.” One of the producers he cited as producing “really star stuff” was Tegan Passalacqua.

I first wrote about Tegan back in 2014, in a World of Fine Wine blog about the world of chenin, pointing for a start to the remarkably different conditions for the grape in its great heartland, the Loire Valley, compared to the Cape. In California, I added, “where chenin blanc has been despised much more than it ever was in the Cape, and is dwindling even faster and with remarkably few ambitious versions, there’s perhaps a hint of revival.” Any such revival, I suggested, “will in the first instance at least, have more to do with the South African example than the French”.

Tegan, winemaker at Turley, had a few years before come out to work a harvest in the Sadie cellar in the Swartland. There, I said, “he acquired something of an obsession with chenin that clearly survived his return to California”. I wondered if “perhaps a chenin revival is heralded in California too”. Now it seems that it’s arrived – a much smaller affair, of course, than the South African blossoming was. Unlike here, most of California’s chenin vineyards were long since pulled out to make way for more lucrative varieties (especially chardonnay and cab at the higher end, and zinfandel for cheap “white zin” at the lower).

The Wine-searcher article on the chenin “renaissance” does talk of South African chenin, and reports, as an example, on the recent retail success in the USA of MAN Family Chenin Blanc and of Lievland’s version, talking to winemaker and part-owner of the brands, José Conde. It’s notable, in fact, that Wine-searcher – internationally important and largely serving a rich US audience, I guess – has shown unusual interest in Cape chenin in recent years.

Its account of “The best Chenin Blancs of 2025” included six Cape and four Loire examples in its top ten list (talking of price and critics’ scores), The six were Sadie Mev Kirsten at no. 2, with Alheit Huilkrans the next Cape example, at 5; Sadie Skurfberg was 6, Mullineux Straw Wine at 7, Stellenrust Mothership at 8 (actually ArtiSons, and easily the least pricey wine on this list at $35); Sadie Rotsbank was at 9.

Very tellingly, however, the Wine-searcher list of not the “best” but the “most wanted” chenins of 2025 (according to users of the website) has only Mev Kirsten and Alheit Cartology in a sea of Loire wines. Prejudice as well as quality is vital and, as I read recently somewhere (but I’m damned if I can remember where), South Africa is “a country that seemingly always has to shout to be heard on the world stage”.

Also in Wine-searcher recently was a remarkably interesting (and positive) overview entitled South Africa and the Quiet Power of Chenin Blanc, by Maria Laura Ortiz. She makes some summary points about chenin well worth quoting here:

  • In Europe, South Africa has established itself as the only credible alternative to France.
  • In the UK, availability is close to parity between the two origins – a rare case where a New World country competes head-to-head in a historically Old World category.
  • In the US, while France remains dominant, South Africa is the only non-European origin with sufficient scale to expand the category meaningfully.

The author adds that “Chenin Blanc is no longer South Africa’s signature grape – it is its structural anchor.” Of all the country’s varietal offerings, she says, “only Chenin Blanc combines scale, pricing power and differentiation simultaneously”.

The warmth of the current American welcome for chenin, as evidenced not only by the continuing Wine-searcher commentary, is fairly recent. I wrote last week about what seems to me the wrong path that the Chenin Challenge in its earlier years encouraged ambitious Cape chenin to take: sweet, ripe, powerful and oaky wines. I’ve just came across an article I wrote in 2012 called “The trouble with the Chenin Blanc Association”, complaining that the Association was then still advancing that style. A recent “Chenin Blanc Unveiled” event had been held in conjunction with Cape Wine 2012, and there were certainly many producers and serious wine drinkers who didn’t like the two styles being pushed: ““Fresh and fruity”, and “Rich and ripe”. I had done some research and found that, for example, only three of the twelve wines being shown could count as properly dry (below 4 grams per litre of residual sugar).

Drier, more refined styles seemed to be being ignored by the Association. I mentioned in that article that Eric Asimov, highly important critic of the New York Times, had recently reported on a tasting of Cape Chenin. On the whole, he hadn’t liked what he tasted (I suppose there wasn’t all that much being imported into America in 2012). He did approve of the Mullineux and Secateurs wines, but too many, he said, “seemed either flabby or dispiriting”. Ken Forrester FMC 2009, for instance, he found to be “sweet, oaky, unbalanced and fatiguing”.

Things have changed, happily, and that style has certainly been eclipsed at the top level. The  Chenin Blanc Association still, however, thinks it adequate to say that the variety “is well known for its rich stylistic diversity, ranging from fresh and easy-drinking to full and rich with oak-barrel fermentation that makes for complex, powerful wines”. Diversity? Is that as far as their thinking goes? Where do Mev Kirsten and Huikrans fit into that formulation – an alternative rather than a continuum?

But that is just one instance of this rather humdrum website faltering in showing the modern history and excitement of the chenin renaissance in South Africa. Tellingly, the site is still (I’ve just checked) calling for entries for its Top 10 Challenge 2026, whose results were announced more than a week ago, and gives results only of last year’s competition. Cape Chenin deserves the best internet representation – for, amongst others, Americans with their interest piqued.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Luke Dale Roberts takes fine dining to the Kalahari
summary:
Luke Dale Roberts has opened Boscia at Tswalu Kalahari, a new fine-dining restaurant built beneath a century-old farmhouse on the 118,000-hectare reserve. Dale Roberts, formerly of The Test Kitchen, is the creative director, with Dillan Kannemeyer, formerly head chef at Roberts’ SALON and with more than seven years at The Pot Luck Club, leads the […]

The post Luke Dale Roberts takes fine dining to the Kalahari appeared first on winemag.
content:
Luke Dale Roberts has opened Boscia at Tswalu Kalahari, a new fine-dining restaurant built beneath a century-old farmhouse on the 118,000-hectare reserve. Dale Roberts, formerly of The Test Kitchen, is the creative director, with Dillan Kannemeyer, formerly head chef at Roberts’ SALON and with more than seven years at The Pot Luck Club, leads the Boscia kitchen.

The five-course menu draws on European and Asian influences and Kalahari ingredients including venison, tsamma melon, Kalahari salt, dates and wild rosemary. Preservation features prominently, with meat sourced largely from a Kalahari butcher. South African wine pairings and non-alcoholic options are available.

The restaurant forms part of the Tswalu guest experience and is included for stays of two nights or more. From October, Boscia will also open to the public for Saturday lunch at R3,850 per person. Bookings open on the first of each month for the following month.

Tswalu is a private reserve in the southern Kalahari owned by the Oppenheimer family. Boscia takes its name from the shepherd’s tree, Boscia albitrunca, which is common on the reserve.

The post Groot Constantia appoints new CEO appeared first on winemag.
content:
Edo Heyns.

Groot Constantia, the commercial wine property held in trust for the nation, has appointed Dr Edo Heyns as CEO, effective 19 October 2026. He will work alongside current CEO Jean Naudé during a handover before Naudé retires on 30 November, having led the estate since 2002. Heyns was CEO of Allée Bleue from March 2024 and previously held senior roles at Advini South Africa. His experience spans wine production, operations, sales, marketing and hospitality.

title: Tim James: A visit to Callie Louw’s Sonkop
summary:
Fans of Callie Louw – there are many, and I think “fan” is the right word – will be pleased to know that all is going well at his new venture. Very well indeed, I’d say after my visit to his farm and nascent winery last week, on a misty spring morning. It’s just more […]

The post Tim James: A visit to Callie Louw’s Sonkop appeared first on winemag.
content:
Fans of Callie Louw – there are many, and I think “fan” is the right word – will be pleased to know that all is going well at his new venture. Very well indeed, I’d say after my visit to his farm and nascent winery last week, on a misty spring morning.

It’s just more than a year since Callie and family arrived here, having left Porseleinberg. There he’d made fifteen vintages of syrah off those vines, and overseen and planted vineyards on this and two other large Swartland properties, all owned by Boekenhoutskloof. It seemed right, as he approached 50, to take the brave and difficult step of working for himself. As he told me at the time: “I’ve always loved farming and owning my own land has been a dream… the fire has grown bigger.”

This new farm – it was called Uitvlucht and has been renamed Sonkop for its highest peak – is in a part of the Swartland that’s remarkably different from Porseleinberg. Rolling hills too, but this is in the Joubertskloof in the low foothills of the Paardeberg, on the other side of that magical mountain from the famous establishments of Sadie, Badenhorst, Lammershoek, David & Nadia et al. With the highest vineyards at about 400 metres, it’s actually more elevated than Porseleinberg. When we drove up to those dizzy heights, Callie assured me that were it not for the mist we’d be able to see right across to Table Mountain.

This is perhaps the prettiest part of the southern Swartland, though lacking the grand vistas of wheatfields and huge open skies with mountains on the horizons. Anyone who knew the Fynbos Estate, home to Johan Simons’s eccentric and occasionally fascinating Dragonridge range of wines, will know this tucked-away area – Sonkop is its neighbouring farm. (A large Rainbow Chickens property is on another side, mostly undeveloped land as far as I could see). 

It’s easy to understand what drew Callie here, even apart from the appealing setting and the attractive buildings, including a good house, amongst large trees. There were already some vineyards planted on the mostly east- but also south-facing slopes, the orientation keeping them a little cooler, less exposed to the afternoon sun. Many vines were virused and needed to be removed (some were grafted to other varieties), but there’s some really good chenin, going back to the 1980s. The farm has a well-sized dam, fed by run-off from the slopes – a significant advantage over the farms of the Aprilskloof and Siebritskloof. Rather too much run-off on rare occasions, in fact – the mighty rains of May this year did fill the dam but also caused some havoc among the bare soils of newly-planted vines.

So. Having lost his viticulturist heart, Callie found a financial partner – always a tricky business, and I gather it took two shots, to find the KwaZulu-Natal wine lover, with some relevant experience in agricutural investment, who is now involved (but keeping his head low for the present it seems). Callie seems very pleased with the arrangements.

Investment in Sonkop is substantial. It’s altogether a much larger proposition than I’d guessed it to be. And larger than Callie had originally thought, in fact. A neighbouring wine-grape farm (devoted to mass production) had come up for sale and Sonkop has shared the land with the recently new owners of the Fynbos estate (things are clearly moving in this sliver of Swartland). These are an Italian-Swiss couple, who are, I gather, more interested in expanding and developing Fynbos’s olive plantations – though they’re not abandoning the vineyards there and, with Callie Louw as a friendly neighbour, can they avoid dabbling in wine too?

Sonkop has, then, a total of some 130 hectares. About 20 hectares of vineyards are now in production – including that old chenin as well as some chardonnay and cabernet sauvignon. Callie has already planted 15 more (shiraz, grenache and more cab), and another 15 will go in next year. White-wine grapes will account for just 12 of the final 50 hectares. Another venture on the farm sees Callie’s wife Marie, a professional photographer, moving to develop a commercial flower garden. Meanwhile, a production cellar is under construction and might just be usable to vinify the grapes that are now mere potential in the vigorous vineyards around it – Callie seems more concerned about getting the paperwork involved in registering it as a wine-production site done in time than the construction logistics.

As to the wines, Callie’s determination is to have just two, expressive of Sonkop and its plantings, and named for it: a red blend – seemingly with a basis in shiraz, and including that surprising cabernet (unorthodox for the modern Swartland) for structural support; and a white blend based on farm’s old chenin. This is a brave ambition; no other significant Swartland producer has managed to achieve this degree of focus – and it’s not the best time in the history of wine to be introducing a new brand, from a fair-sized large farm, with just two wines.

The first Sonkops will be vintage 2026. Callie made them in the cellars of Vondeling, where he is also helping with the wines and vineyards (he doesn’t like the word “consultant”). There they are resting and maturing – sadly I didn’t get a glance or a taste on this visit. Vintage 2027 will, hopefully, be accomplished in the new cellar. The labels for the two Sonkops are being designed now: they will reflect the view of the mountain and vineyards, and the image will, as I understand it, develop in detail and completeness over the next decade as the new vineyards come into maturity.

Callie has been working hard here, and effectively, and there is much more to come – he has, says his friend and former employer Marc Kent, “a work ethic second to none”. When he was showing me the vineyards he’d planted, his pleasure and anticipation was almost palpable as he welcomed the new spring growth of his emerging vines.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Greg Sherwood MW: 2021 – the Cape’s next great Cab vintage
summary:
If you have been following numerous wine commentators and wine social media accounts of late, you would have found it pretty difficult to miss all the debates comparing the 2015 to the 2017 vintage in the Cape. Without a question of a doubt, both are vintages that are developing into two of South Africa’s most […]

The post Greg Sherwood MW: 2021 – the Cape’s next great Cab vintage appeared first on winemag.
content:
If you have been following numerous wine commentators and wine social media accounts of late, you would have found it pretty difficult to miss all the debates comparing the 2015 to the 2017 vintage in the Cape.

Without a question of a doubt, both are vintages that are developing into two of South Africa’s most revered and collectable. As 2017 hits the ten-year mark in a few months’ time, this debate is sure to intensify further – the ten-year landmark normally regarded as a key quality marker for assessing the Cape’s top reds.

Indeed, I’d be lying if I said I wasn’t also quite drawn to a recent blind tasting held by famous South African sommelier, Higgo Jacobs, where he compared the 2015 and the 2017 releases of Meerlust Rubicon, Stark Condé Three Pines, Kanonkop Paul Sauer and Glenelly Lady May Cape Bordeaux blends. At nine years and eleven years old respectively, it seems a good time to make some new ageing assessments as many consumers and collectors alike will be thinking about starting to pull corks, if they haven’t started doing so already.

2015 vs 2017: The debate continues

Looking at the results, they certainly seemed to be inconclusive. The Meerlust Rubicon 2015 – a legendary wine – was considered “cracking” and preferred to the 2017. The Stark Condé Three Pines 2015 was also preferred over the 2017. For the Kanonkop Paul Sauer, the adjudication was a little closer, the 2017 Paul Sauer just pipping the famous Tim Atkin MW 100-point 2015, though both were noted as being the “wines of the night.” Finally, the exceptional 2017 Lady May was also preferred over the 2015, but it was noted that the wines both shared many similarities.

The conclusions drawn from this little tasting was that the differences between the two vintages, when tasted blind, was not as easy to distinguish as would be expected. More importantly, out of the eight wines, all were considered still in an upward trajectory of development and can, or should, be cellared for longer. Both vintages are living up to expectations as collectable fine wines for the long haul.

2021 – the next one to watch

But with very few of these wines still on the market, I thought it would be far more helpful and insightful for Winemag.co.za readers to highlight another recent tasting I went to in London – The Cabernet Collective’s Stellenbosch Vintage 2021 Tasting – held at the ‘new’ mecca of South African fine dining and fine wine, Kudu Restaurant at 7 Moxon Street, Marylebone. (Do pop in for lunch or dinner if you are visiting London, and ask for Brian Tapera, the very capable Zimbabwean sommelier!)

For those that don’t know, the Stellenbosch Cabernet Collective is a group of Stellenbosch producers brought together with the aim of “curating the expression of Stellenbosch through Cabernet Sauvignon”. They are joined together in sharing passion, discovery and knowledge. “It is to Stellenbosch that we look for the classic and elegant Cabernet Sauvignons that sit comfortably on the global stage, shoulder to shoulder with the world’s most revered wines,” organizer Billie Lambrechts will tell you.

As a reminder, the 2020 post-harvest period was characterised by very hot and dry conditions, which led to early leaf fall, especially in early ripening cultivars. The winter rainfall started late, but regular cold fronts contributed almost 100mm more precipitation than in the previous season. The budding period was particularly cool and wet, and low soil temperatures delayed bud break by up to 14 days, with bud break for later cultivars such as Cabernet Sauvignon developing evenly.

Despite sustained cool conditions, the flowering and fruit set periods were moderate and ideal. Véraison followed the seasonal trend and was generally up to 14 days later than the previous season. Ripening was consistently about 10-14 days later than the previous year, and the ripening period was very moderate. This resulted in good hang times, minimal harvesting pressure and allowed for optimal picking.

Although yields were lower, the grape compositions and preliminary wine quality of the 2021 vintage showed immediate promise. Despite the cooler conditions, the red cultivars generally achieved ideal sugar and alcohol levels, with lower pHs and higher acidities than in other recent seasons. The wines, overall, have intensity and freshness coupled with very fine, linear tannin structures – all the building blocks for yet another excellent, ageworthy Cape vintage.

Top five

1 – Tied

Le Riche Reserve 2021, 14.5% – Dense and intense, perfumed with cassis and violets, salty crème de cassis, black cherries and dusty stony minerality. Full and impressive in the mouth, satin texture with a bold concentration, plush mineral tannins and a focused, powerful finish. Wow! True class. 97/100 GSMW

1 – Tied

Thelema Mountain Vineyards Cabernet Sauvignon 2021, 14% Abv. – Beautifully seductive perfume of violets, black currants and black cherry kirsch liquor. Super polished marble tannins, tight knit, fine grained and simply delicious. Well integrated acids lend extra frame and linearity before a tart, vibrant, tangy black berry laden finish. Simply benchmark! 97/100 GSMW

2

Oldenburg Rondekop Per Se 2021, 14.64% Abv. – This is a classy, slightly broody expression of top-class Cab, showing violet and white flower perfume, notable minerality and layers of earthy black berry fruits, saline cassis, cherry pipe tobacco, and delicate cedar notes. The palate is taut and polished, effortlessly weightless and bright with a tight grained classy finessed finish. Very smart indeed. 96+/100 GSMW

3 – Tied

Meerlust 2021, 13.7% Abv. – Tight and broody, this has closed up into a more mineral expression with graphite and cedar, crushed stones, black berries and black orchard fruits. Sleek and subtle, this suggests a lot but is holding back the full fireworks. Texture of silk, fabulous tension and beautifully fine-grained tannins with a wet stone minerality on the finish. Very serious and seriously classy. 96/100 GSMW

3 – Tied

Bellevue Reserve 2021, 14% Abv. – Rich exotic black fruits layer the palate supported by an attractive perfume of violets, cherry blossom and sweet blueberries. The palate is so polished and fine with chalky tannins, a super fine-grained texture and a harmonious focused finish. Real class. 96/100 GSMW

4

Delaire Graff Reserve 2021, 14.8% Abv. – A masterclass from Morne Vrey, this is complex and multi-dimensional with aromatics of cigar box, oyster shell, graphite and kelp over salty black currant notes. Super polished and sleek, the palate is elegantly fleshy and opulent with a pinpoint focus, chalky granitic tannins, and a cool, taut mineral finish. A very grown-up expression. 95+/100 GSMW

5 – Tied

Cavalli 2021, Helderberg, 14.55% Abv. – Exoticly perfumed nose with violets and white blossoms, red and black currants and subtle hints of sour plum. Cool, creamy and silky with sweet tannins, a delightful tight grained tension, and a pitch perfect balance on the spicy finish. Delightful. 95/100 GSMW

5 – Tied

Journey’s End V4 2021, Helderberg, 14% Abv. – Classical aromatics with violets and cedar spice, potpourri and black currant fruit notes. Silky mouthfeel, real precision and focus, satin tannins but tight knit with an intense persistent concentration on the mineral-laden finish. Top Drawer kit. 95/100 GSMW

Best of the rest:

Alto 2021, Helderberg, 14.5% Abv. – 94+/100 GSMW

Ernie Els Wines Major Series 2021, Helderberg, 13.95% Abv. – 94+/100 GSMW

Rust en Vrede 2021, Helderberg, 14% Abv. – 94+/100 GSMW

Klein Graniet 2021, 14% Abv. – 94+/100 GSMW

Le Riche 2021, Faure, 14.39% Abv. – 94/100 GSMW

Avontuur The West Peak 2021, 14.34% Abv. – 93+/100 GSMW

Waterford 2021, 13.5% Abv. – 93+/100 GSMW

  • Greg Sherwood was born in Pretoria, South Africa, and as the son of a career diplomat, spent his first 21 years traveling the globe with his parents. With a Business Management and Marketing degree from Webster University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA, Sherwood began his working career as a commodity trader. In 2000, he decided to make more of a long-held interest in wine taking a position at Handford Wines in South Kensington, London, working his way up to the position of Senior Wine Buyer over 22 years. Sherwood currently consults to a number of top fine wine merchants in London while always keeping one eye firmly on the South African wine industry. He qualified as the 303rd Master of Wine in 2007.

title: NFB Old Vine Report 2026: Call for entries
summary:

The post NFB Old Vine Report 2026: Call for entries appeared first on winemag.
content:
Entries for the third annual Old Vine Report are now open, with NFB Private Wealth Management, established in 1985, joining as sponsor.

Wines must be made from Certified Heritage Vineyards (vines that are 35 years and older vines registered with SAWIS and approved by the Old Vine Project).

The report will be based on the outcome of a blind tasting of wines entered within a specific category and includes key findings, tasting notes for the Top 10 wines, buyer’s guide and scores on the 100-point quality scale for all wines entered.

Wines will be tasted by a three-person panel consisting of Christian Eedes as chairman, James Pietersen, CEO of of Wine Cellar, Cape Town merchants and cellarers of fine wine, and Francois Rautenbach, a hospitality and wine specialist, scoring done according to the 100-point system.
